case.source: Derived from https://x.com/stanine/status/2084385000959701146 (Matt MacInnis, 2026-08-03). Prompts, targets, and rubrics are ours.
case.prompt:
Review this paragraph and rewrite the lines that need it. It is the opening of an internal design doc; nothing precedes it and no earlier recommendation or reason was given.

My actual recommendation is to ship the migration behind a flag. The real reason is that the backfill takes eleven hours and cannot be paused once it starts. The key issue is deciding who owns the rollback.
case.expected_output: A critique that flags 'actual', 'real', and 'key' as modifiers carrying no information about their nouns, names the false implication each creates about alternatives the reader was never given, and repairs by deleting the modifier rather than substituting another adjective or adding an explanatory clause.
assertions: Flags at least two of 'actual recommendation', 'real reason', 'key issue' as modifiers that can be deleted without changing what the sentence says.
Names the false implication: 'actual' and 'real' imply an earlier recommendation or reason was offered and was not the genuine one, when nothing precedes this paragraph.
Does not excuse the modifiers on the grounds that the surrounding sentence already names a concrete mechanism (eleven-hour backfill, no pause once started, rollback owner).
Repairs by deletion ('My recommendation', 'The reason', 'The issue') rather than by substituting another adjective or expanding into a clause that justifies the modifier.

graded_dimensions.name: implicature-naming
graded_dimensions.rubric: 5 = states what the modifier falsely implies about alternatives the reader was never shown; 3 = calls the word vague, filler, or unnecessary without naming the implication; 1 = does not flag it.

graded_dimensions.name: repair-by-deletion
graded_dimensions.rubric: 5 = every repair is a deletion and each line gets shorter; 3 = swaps in a different modifier or keeps one hollow modifier; 1 = expands the line to justify the modifier.

case.source: Derived from https://x.com/stanine/status/2084385000959701146 (Matt MacInnis, 2026-08-03). Prompts, targets, and rubrics are ours.
case.prompt:
Review this reply an assistant wrote. The user's entire message was: 'why is the deploy slow?' The user did not mention Docker or the build at any point.

It would be easy to assume the slowness comes from the Docker build. But the build is not the problem. The problem is that the readiness probe waits a fixed 30 seconds before its first check, so every rollout pays that delay once per pod.
case.expected_output: A critique that flags the invented opposing view: the assistant introduced the Docker-build hypothesis itself and then refuted it, and because no one raised it the contrast is manufactured. The repair is to cut the invented premise, not to keep it (earned) and not to supply evidence for it (the compressed-antithesis repair). The rewrite states the readiness-probe finding directly.
assertions: Flags 'It would be easy to assume the slowness comes from the Docker build' as an opposing view the assistant introduced itself and the user never raised.
Does not grade the 'not the problem / the problem is' contrast as earned antithesis on the grounds that the immediately preceding sentence supplies the Docker-build side.
Does not repair by evidencing the Docker-build side; the invented premise is cut, not supported.
Rewrite deletes the invented setup and states the readiness-probe mechanism directly, keeping the fixed 30-second wait and the per-pod cost.
Rewrite does not substitute a different negation or X-not-Y construction in place of the one it removed.

graded_dimensions.name: strawman-attribution
graded_dimensions.rubric: 5 = names that the assistant planted the alternative itself and that no one raised it; 3 = flags the contrast as unearned or decorative without identifying who introduced the alternative; 1 = grades the contrast as earned because the prior sentence set it up.

graded_dimensions.name: repair-directness
graded_dimensions.rubric: 5 = the rewrite opens on the probe mechanism with no negation retained; 3 = drops the setup but keeps a negation; 1 = keeps the assume-then-refute structure.

case.prompt: Rewrite without AI slop: The true benefit of the new scheduler is that it gives teams genuine visibility into the actual state of every job.
case.expected_output: Deletes 'true', 'genuine', and 'actual' without substituting other adjectives, and returns a shorter sentence. Because the source names no mechanism behind 'visibility', the rewrite keeps the plain claim or marks the missing specifics ask-author; it must not invent a metric, screen, or refresh interval.
assertions: Removes 'true', 'genuine', and 'actual'.
Does not substitute replacement adjectives ('real', 'complete', 'full', 'clear', 'live') for the deleted ones.
Returns a sentence no longer than the input in word count.

graded_dimensions.name: length-control
graded_dimensions.rubric: 5 = shorter than the input; 3 = same length; 1 = longer than the input.

graded_dimensions.name: deletion-fidelity

case.prompt:
Rewrite this opening paragraph of a release note. Nothing precedes it, and the reader has been told nothing about pricing or billing.

This release is not about pricing. It is not a rewrite of the billing stack either. It is about giving you a way to see which queries are slow: the dashboard now groups queries by normalized shape and sorts each group by total time.

Opens on the concrete mechanism (normalized query shape, sorted by total time) instead of on a negation.
Does not substitute another X-not-Y, 'not just X but Y', or 'this is about X rather than Y' construction.
Does not invent a reason the reader might have expected a pricing or billing change.

graded_dimensions.name: strawman-removal
graded_dimensions.rubric: 5 = both invented alternatives are gone and no replacement negation appears; 3 = one removed or one swapped for a different negation; 1 = the not-X framing survives.

graded_dimensions.name: length-control
graded_dimensions.rubric: 5 = shorter than the input while keeping the grouping and sorting mechanism; 3 = same length; 1 = longer.

case.prompt:
Review this launch-post paragraph for AI-writing tells:

We spent three months rewriting the sync engine. That's the whole story. The new engine survived our chaos tests, and that's not nothing. The punchline is that nobody will notice. Sit with that for a moment.
case.expected_output: A critique that flags significance compression (whole story / not nothing / punchline) and therapy voice (sit with that), then rewrites with the mechanism the paragraph is withholding: what the rewrite changed and what the chaos tests actually showed.
assertions: Identifies at least two of 'that's the whole story', 'that's not nothing', 'the punchline is', and 'sit with that' as canned significance or therapy cadence rather than earned emphasis.
Notes that each flagged line asserts weight while withholding the mechanism: what changed in the sync engine, what the chaos tests injected or measured, why users will not notice.
Provides a concrete rewrite that names a mechanism or measurement instead of replacing one canned closer with another.

graded_dimensions.name: mechanism-recovery
graded_dimensions.rubric: 5 = rewrite states what the engine now does under a named failure (retry, replay, conflict rule) or a test result; 3 = removes the cadence but stays abstract; 1 = swaps in a different canned closer.

case.source: Pattern family adapted from simonw/tools llm-cliche-highlighter.html (Apache-2.0, Simon Willison); see docs/deterministic-graders.md for provenance.
case.prompt:
Review this blog intro:

Let's be honest: most migration guides are useless. I won't pretend ours was painless. But here's the thing: the schema change took four hours, not four weeks. Turns out the scary part was renaming a column.
case.expected_output: A critique that flags the candor performance and stage-managed reveals, keeps the two concrete facts (four hours, column rename), and rewrites so the facts open the intro.
assertions: Flags 'Let's be honest', 'I won't pretend', 'here's the thing', and/or 'Turns out' as performative honesty or stage management: sincerity and revelation announced rather than shown.
Preserves the two concrete facts (the four-hour schema change, the column rename) rather than cutting them along with the cadence.
Rewrite opens on the concrete fact instead of a candor announcement and does not introduce a replacement tic such as 'Look,' or 'The truth is'.

case.source: Pattern family adapted from simonw/tools llm-cliche-highlighter.html (Apache-2.0, Simon Willison); see docs/deterministic-graders.md for provenance.
case.prompt:
Review this postmortem excerpt for rhythm tells:

Maybe the alert was too noisy. Maybe the runbook was stale. Maybe nobody was on call. Do we know which? Do we even want to know? The pager fired; the fix didn't.
case.expected_output: A critique that names the structural cadences (the Maybe anaphora run, the stacked questions, the stranded-auxiliary reversal) and rewrites the speculation into verified findings with evidence.
assertions: Identifies the three-sentence 'Maybe ...' run, the stacked rhetorical questions, and the bare-auxiliary reversal ('the fix didn't') as structural cadence carrying uncertainty the postmortem should have resolved.
Notes that a postmortem should replace speculation cadence with what was checked: which of the three hypotheses was tested and what the evidence showed.
Rewrite states at least one verified finding (alert volume, runbook staleness, or the on-call gap) as a plain claim with its evidence, not as a question or a 'Maybe'.

case.source: Pattern family adapted from simonw/tools llm-cliche-highlighter.html (Apache-2.0, Simon Willison); see docs/deterministic-graders.md for provenance.
case.prompt: Review and rewrite this README opener: Zero config, batteries included, and it just works. The whole API is small enough to fit in your head. No wrappers, no lock-in, no surprises.
case.expected_output: A critique that flags the dev-blog boilerplate and the negation chain, then rewrites with checkable specifics: what the default configuration actually is, what ships in the box, what size the API surface is.
assertions: Flags 'zero config', 'batteries included', 'it just works', and 'fit in your head' as stock simplicity claims that assert instead of demonstrating.
Flags the 'No wrappers, no lock-in, no surprises' chain as a claim list with no verifiable referent, distinct from a factual negation list.
Rewrites with checkable specifics (the actual defaults, a count of public functions or types, what a first call looks like) or recommends cutting the line.

graded_dimensions.name: checkability
graded_dimensions.rubric: 5 = every kept claim is verifiable from the README or code (a default, a count, a command); 3 = mixed; 1 = boilerplate swapped for new boilerplate.

case.source: Pattern family adapted from simonw/tools llm-cliche-highlighter.html (Apache-2.0, Simon Willison); see docs/deterministic-graders.md for provenance.
case.prompt:
Review this team retro summary:

We shipped two weeks late. That loss is real, and it's worth naming. You already know why: scope creep. Sit with the discomfort before we plan the next cycle.
case.expected_output: A critique that flags the counselor cadence, keeps the two facts (two-week slip, scope creep), and rewrites into a retro item that names or asks for the specific scope additions.
assertions: Flags 'worth naming', 'you already know', and 'sit with the discomfort' as therapy-voice cadence performing reflection instead of doing it.
Keeps the substantive content, the two-week slip and scope creep, and asks for the specific mid-cycle additions behind it.
Rewrite states the slip, names or requests the concrete scope change, and proposes a check for the next cycle, without the counselor framing.

case.source: Pattern family adapted from simonw/tools llm-cliche-highlighter.html (Apache-2.0, Simon Willison); see docs/deterministic-graders.md for provenance.
case.prompt: Rewrite without AI slop: We rebuilt the editor. No sign-ups, no downloads, no hassle. Zero config — it just works. Let's be honest: most editors are bloated. This one fits in your head. That's the whole point.
case.expected_output: A short launch paragraph whose claims are concrete and checkable: what runs where, what setup a first use actually requires, what size the feature surface is.
assertions: Removes the negation chain, the boilerplate ('zero config', 'it just works', 'fits in your head'), the candor opener, and the significance-compression closer.
States at least one checkable specific: where the editor runs, what a first use requires, or a concrete measure of its size or scope.
Does not substitute new prestige abstractions or a replacement cadence such as 'it's not an editor, it's a philosophy'.

graded_dimensions.name: specificity
graded_dimensions.rubric: 5 = names where it runs, what setup is required, or a measured size; 3 = concrete-sounding but unverifiable; 1 = boilerplate swapped for boilerplate.

graded_dimensions.name: length-control
graded_dimensions.rubric: 5 = same or shorter word count than input; 1 = inflated rewrite.

case.source: Pattern family adapted from simonw/tools llm-cliche-highlighter.html (Apache-2.0, Simon Willison); see docs/deterministic-graders.md for provenance.
case.prompt: Rewrite without AI slop: Turns out nobody read the runbook. Here's the kicker: the alert fired twice and was acked twice. Do I wish we'd caught it sooner? Do I wish the escalation had worked? That's not nothing, and the on-call rotation is dead.
case.expected_output: Plain incident prose: what happened in order, with the double ack and the escalation gap stated as findings and a concrete follow-up.
assertions: Removes the reveal framing ('Turns out', 'Here's the kicker'), the stacked rhetorical questions, the 'not nothing' hedge, and the 'is dead' obituary.
States the facts as ordered findings: the runbook was not consulted, the alert fired and was acknowledged twice, the escalation did not happen.
Ends with a concrete follow-up (a runbook link in the alert payload, an escalation timeout, an ownership change) rather than a verdict about the rotation.

case.expected_output: Keeps the sentence. The reversal is earned: the evidence (flame graph, 61%, arena fix) arrives in the same breath as the claim.

case.source: Over-flagging guard for the structural sentence-anaphora detector (simonw/tools, Apache-2.0): repeated openers can carry a real dependency chain.
case.prompt: Review this design-doc passage: Every request carries a trace id. Every trace id maps to exactly one tenant. Every tenant pins to exactly one shard. That chain is what makes cross-tenant reads impossible by construction.
case.expected_output: Keeps the passage. The repeated 'Every ...' opener tracks an invariant chain, each sentence adding one link that the conclusion depends on.
assertions: Does not flag the repeated 'Every ...' openers as decorative anaphora; recognizes that each sentence adds one link in an invariant chain the final sentence relies on.
If rewriting, preserves the three invariants and their order rather than merging them into one abstract sentence.

case.source: Over-flagging guard for the performative-honesty family (simonw/tools, Apache-2.0).
case.prompt: Review this API deprecation note: To be clear, the v1 endpoints are unchanged: every route returns the same schema as before, and the deprecation affects only the beta batch endpoint.
case.expected_output: Keeps the sentence. 'To be clear' is followed by the clarification it announces, with named referents (v1 schema, beta batch endpoint).
assertions: Does not treat 'To be clear' as performative honesty here, because the sentence delivers the scoping clarification it announces.
Any edit keeps the scoping facts; trimming the opener is acceptable, but rejecting the sentence as slop is not.

case.source: Failure pattern named by Shane Littrell (@MetacogniShane), https://x.com/MetacogniShane/status/2092638724915896675, 2026-08-26.
case.prompt:
Review this passage:

Most teams treat retries as a solved problem. Here's what most people get wrong. Retrying is harder than it looks, and getting it right matters more than teams realise. The consequences of getting it wrong can be severe.
case.expected_output: Flags "Here's what most people get wrong." as a cataphoric teaser: it promises withheld content that no following sentence discharges. The two sentences after it restate that retries are hard and assert severity without naming a failure mode. Recommends cutting the teaser, or escalating to ask-author for the specific retry failure, rather than inventing one.
assertions: Flags "Here's what most people get wrong." as a forward-pointing promise that the passage never discharges.

Names that the sentences after the teaser restate the difficulty instead of supplying the withheld content — no named failure mode such as duplicate side effects, a thundering herd, or a non-idempotent write.
Either cuts the teaser and keeps the plain claim or escalates to ask-author for the specific failure mode; does not invent a concrete retry bug the source does not supply.

graded_dimensions.name: discharge-diagnosis
graded_dimensions.rubric: 5 = states which sentence should have discharged the promise and shows it does not; 3 = flags the teaser as generic slop without the discharge test; 1 = does not flag it.

graded_dimensions.name: non-invention
graded_dimensions.rubric: 5 = supplies no retry failure mode absent from the source; 3 = one borderline added specific; 1 = fabricates a concrete bug to fill the rewrite slot.

case.prompt:
Review these two sentences:

Here's where it gets interesting: the cache is what makes the whole thing fast. Without the cache, it would be slower.
case.expected_output: Flags the teaser because the payoff restates the tease. "Without the cache, it would be slower" is the same claim as "the cache makes it fast," so the promised interest was supplied by the frame, not by the content. Recommends cutting the teaser and naming what the cache actually does, or cutting the pair.
assertions: Flags "Here's where it gets interesting:" as a forward-pointing promise whose payoff does not deliver the promised content.
Identifies that the discharging sentence restates the first one rather than adding anything, so the interest is asserted by the frame instead of earned by the payload.
Does not treat a synonym swap for "interesting" as the fix.

case.source: Shape variant catalogued by tropes.fyi as "The X? A Y."; see docs/cataphoric-teaser-prior-art.md.
case.prompt:
Review this passage:

We moved the indexer to a Tuesday deploy window. The result? Not what we expected. The team spent the rest of the week on it.
case.expected_output: Flags "The result? Not what we expected." as a cataphoric teaser wearing a different shape: a self-posed question answered by a fragment that withholds the answer. "The team spent the rest of the week on it" reports that there was trouble without naming it, so the promise is not discharged. Recommends stating the result or escalating to ask-author.
assertions: Flags "The result? Not what we expected." as a forward-pointing promise the passage does not discharge — the following sentence reports that there was trouble without naming what it was.

Recognizes the self-posed-question-plus-fragment shape as the same failure as an explicit "Here's what..." teaser, rather than treating it as ordinary sentence variety or as a staccato-contrast finding.
Recommends stating the result or escalating to ask-author, and does not invent what went wrong with the indexer.

case.source: Boundary between the discharge test and novelty inflation; see docs/cataphoric-teaser-prior-art.md → "Scarcity claims are a second, independent defect".
case.prompt:
Review this passage:

Here's what nobody tells you about connection pooling: size the pool to the database's max connections, not to your worker count. Teams that size it to worker count exhaust the server under load.
case.expected_output: Two findings that must be kept apart. The forward reference IS discharged — the clause after the colon names the specific rule and the next sentence names the failure — so this is not an undischarged teaser. The "Here's what nobody tells you" frame is still wrong, on separate grounds: it asserts the knowledge is rare, which the passage does not support and which the commonplace nature of the advice contradicts. Cut the frame, keep the content.
assertions: Recognizes that the forward reference is discharged — the clause after the colon names the specific sizing rule and the following sentence names the failure mode — and so does not flag it as an undischarged or unpaid-off teaser.
Still flags the "Here's what nobody tells you" frame, on separate grounds from discharge: it claims the knowledge is rare, a claim about the world the passage does not support.
Recommends cutting the frame while keeping the discharged content, rather than cutting the passage, rewriting the sizing rule, or demanding more specificity.

case.source: Failure pattern named by Shane Littrell (@MetacogniShane), https://x.com/MetacogniShane/status/2092638724915896675, 2026-08-26; the saturation reading follows Paul Bloom, https://substack.com/@smallpotatoes/note/c-322302112.
case.prompt:
Rewrite this section without AI slop:

Here's the part nobody tells you about on-call: the pager is not the problem. The problem is what happens after.

But here's where it gets interesting. Most teams write a postmortem and move on. Few of them change the alert.

And here's what most people get wrong about alert tuning. It is not a one-time task.
case.expected_output: A rewrite that drops all three teaser openers, keeps the two concrete claims (a postmortem gets written but the alert is never changed; alert tuning is recurring work), and does not substitute another forward-pointing hook or an X-not-Y cadence for the teasers it removed.
assertions: Removes all three cataphoric teaser openers: "Here's the part nobody tells you", "here's where it gets interesting", and "here's what most people get wrong".

Preserves the concrete content — the postmortem that gets written while the alert stays unchanged, and alert tuning as recurring rather than one-time work — instead of deleting it along with the teasers.
Does not substitute another forward-pointing hook ("But there's a catch", "The real problem?", "What happens next") or an X-not-Y cadence in the rewrite.

graded_dimensions.name: teaser-removal
graded_dimensions.rubric: 5 = all three teasers gone and none replaced by another forward hook; 3 = one survives or one is swapped for a different hook; 1 = the teaser scaffolding is preserved or restyled.

graded_dimensions.name: content-preservation
graded_dimensions.rubric: 5 = both concrete claims survive the cut; 3 = one is lost or blurred; 1 = the rewrite keeps the shape and drops the content.

graded_dimensions.name: length-control
graded_dimensions.rubric: 5 = same or shorter word count than input; 1 = inflated rewrite.

case.source: Boundary case: discharge is necessary but not sufficient. Adjacent pattern is `conorbronsdon/avoid-ai-writing`'s "emotional flatline"; see docs/cataphoric-teaser-prior-art.md.
case.prompt:
Rewrite without AI slop:

What surprised me most about the migration was the rollback. We had budgeted a week for it. It took forty minutes, because the old schema was still live behind a feature flag.
case.expected_output: The forward reference here IS discharged, and specifically — so passing the discharge test is not enough to keep it. The budgeted-week against forty-minutes gap is the surprise, and the feature flag explains it, so announcing the surprise first tells the reader what to feel before showing them why. The rewrite cuts the frame and keeps both the contrast and the mechanism.
assertions: Removes the "What surprised me most" pre-announcement rather than keeping it on the grounds that the following sentences discharge it.
Preserves both the budgeted-week against forty-minutes contrast and the feature-flag mechanism that explains it.
Does not substitute another forward-pointing frame ("Here's the surprising part", "The kicker?", "And then something unexpected happened") and does not add a detail the source does not supply.

graded_dimensions.name: frame-removal
graded_dimensions.rubric: 5 = the significance announcement is gone and nothing forward-pointing replaces it; 3 = softened or swapped for a different frame; 1 = kept because it was discharged.

graded_dimensions.name: content-preservation
graded_dimensions.rubric: 5 = week-vs-forty-minutes and the feature flag both survive; 3 = one is lost or blurred; 1 = the rewrite keeps the frame's shape and drops the specifics.

graded_dimensions.name: length-control
graded_dimensions.rubric: 5 = same or shorter word count than input; 1 = inflated rewrite.

case.prompt:
Review this line from a methods section:

We report three robustness checks: held-out scoring, a paired bootstrap, and a sign-flip permutation test.
case.expected_output: Keeps the line. The colon is a cataphoric label and the promise is discharged inside the same sentence by the three named checks. Forward reference is not a teaser when the payload arrives.
assertions: Does not flag "We report three robustness checks:" as a cataphoric teaser, engagement bait, or artificial suspense.
Names that the promise is discharged in the same sentence by the three specific checks.
Does not recommend removing the colon or expanding the enumeration into prose.

case.prompt:
Review this paragraph:

So why did the queue drain in twenty minutes instead of two hours? The consumer had been running with prefetch=1 since the March deploy. Raising it to 50 cut the round-trip wait per message from 40ms to under 1ms.
case.expected_output: Keeps the opening question. It points forward, but the next two sentences discharge it with a named cause (prefetch=1 since the March deploy) and a measured effect (40ms to under 1ms). A rhetorical question is a teaser only when the answer does not arrive.
assertions: Does not flag the opening question as a cataphoric teaser, clickbait, or artificial suspense.
Names that the following two sentences discharge the question with a specific cause and a measured effect.
Does not recommend converting the question into a declarative topic sentence merely to remove the forward reference.

case.source: Precision guard against the anaphoric mirror; see docs/cataphoric-teaser-prior-art.md → "Direction: cataphoric versus anaphoric".
case.prompt:
Review this passage:

We tried three fixes: a bigger pool, a read replica, and a per-tenant queue. That last one is the counterintuitive one. Per-tenant queuing costs more in idle workers but removes the noisy-neighbour stall.
case.expected_output: The significance label points backward at an item already named, so it is not a cataphoric teaser. A critique may still flag it as redundant — the sentence after it supplies the mechanism the label was claiming — but the diagnosis must be back-pointing, not a withheld payload. The opening colon is a cataphoric label discharged by its own enumeration and should not be flagged at all.
assertions: Does not classify "That last one is the counterintuitive one." as a cataphoric teaser, forward reference, or withheld payoff; if it flags the line at all, it identifies it as pointing back at an item already named.
Does not flag "We tried three fixes:" — the colon is discharged by the enumeration in the same sentence.
Notes that the following sentence supplies the mechanism (idle-worker cost against the noisy-neighbour stall), so any flag on the label concerns redundancy rather than a missing payload.

case.source: Discourse deixis as defined in Blom & Hansen 2015; see docs/cataphoric-teaser-prior-art.md.
case.prompt:
Review this line from the top of a long design doc:

The rest of this document walks through the three failure modes in the order we hit them: lease expiry, duplicate delivery, and clock skew.
case.expected_output: Keeps the line. It refers to the document itself rather than to content — discourse deixis — but the promise is discharged in the same sentence by the three named failure modes and their ordering. Self-referential signposting is a teaser only when the payload does not arrive.
assertions: Does not flag the line as a cataphoric teaser, engagement bait, manufactured suspense, or throat-clearing.
Names that although the sentence points at the document rather than at content, the promise is discharged in the same sentence by the three named failure modes.
Distinguishes it from an undischarged signpost such as "Read on to find out what went wrong," instead of treating roadmap sentences as slop by shape.
